alt: A flowchart: delete the context sentence and ask whether your reading of the quotation is weaker. If yes, the context is a lens that explains the writer’s choice or changes a moment’s meaning, so keep it. If no, it is decoration, so cut it.
caption: Context earns AO4 only when it changes how a moment reads.

alt: Two timelines. The Scarlet Letter is set in seventeenth-century Boston, published in 1850 and read now. Great Expectations was published in 1860–61 but looks back to the earlier part of the century. Dashed arrows show each writer looking backwards.
caption: The gap between setting and writing is often the best AO4 question to ask.

alt: A paragraph on Charlotte Lucas’s decision to marry Mr Collins split into three parts: an AO1 point that marriage could be a practical bargain, an AO2 method of calm statements and structural contrast with Elizabeth, and AO4 context about a woman of Charlotte’s class. An arrow shows the context explaining the method.
caption: The context explains the method, inside the same paragraph.

after: ## Worked example 2: improving a bolt-on sentence
alt: Top: a bolt-on version puts a sentence on dark imagery next to a sentence on the divine right of kings, with no link. Bottom: the integrated version runs from Macbeth asking the stars to hide their light, through an audience who believed a king was chosen by God, to the argument that he knows the murder is sacrilege.
caption: Context should explain the imagery and drive the argument.
